payload.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
payload.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
payload.holding: The Court held that the multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased, future prospects must be awarded even for fixed/self-employed income based on standardized percentages, and the Court has the power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.
payload.ratio: In motor accident compensation claims under Section 166 of the MV Act, the multiplier must be selected based on the age of the deceased rather than the claimants, future prospects apply to fixed-salary and self-employed individuals, and appellate courts are obligated under Order XLI Rule 33 and the concept of just compensation to correct and enhance inadequate awards.

Applying the degree test, the Supreme Court has first held that even in the cases of death of a person
in a motor accident who was either self-employed or was working on a fixed salary, an addition (to
loss of income) has to be made towards future prospects. Second, it has been held that
compensation on account of future prospects in such case may be computed at the rate of 40% of the
established income in case of the age of the deceased being below 40 years; at the rate of 25% of the
established income in the case of the age of the deceased between 40 to 50 years and at the rate of
10% in case of age of the deceased being between 50 to 60 years.
The term established income has also been clarified to mean the income minus the tax component.
Question and occasion to examine tax payability arises only if there is a real income. Therefore,
clearly, claim for future prospects would arise only in cases where the claimants are successful in
establishing any amount of definite income earned by the deceased. As a corollary to that, future
prospects may not be awarded in cases of notional income as such income can never be categorised
as established income, it having never been actually and factually earned and it being not real.

args.question: Which judgments apply future prospects under Pranay Sethi, and at what percentage?
args.answer:
## Judgments Applying Future Prospects Under *Pranay Sethi* (National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi, (2017) 16 SCC 680)

The corpus contains **6 judgments** that actually apply the future prospects percentages laid down in *Pranay Sethi*. A further 2 judgments cite *Pranay Sethi* but do **not** apply future prospects (the claimants failed to prove established income). Here is the breakdown:

---

### A. Judgments THAT APPLY future prospects percentages

| # | Doc ID | Case Name | Court | Deceased/Injured Age | Employment Type | % Applied | Basis |
|---|--------|-----------|-------|---------------------|----------------|-----------|-------|
| 1 | **doc_041** | *No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... v. No.1* | MACT, Bangalore | Below 40 years | Stable employment (regular income) | **50%** | *Pranay Sethi* para 61(iii) — permanent job, below 40 |
| 2 | **doc_019** | *Surendra Singh v. Vijay Singh* | Allahabad HC | 23 years (first case) / 27 years (second case) | Fixed salary (private employment) | **40%** | *Pranay Sethi* para 61(iv) — self-employed/fixed salary, below 40 |
| 3 | **doc_020** | *Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria v. Dilipkumar Ranchhodbhai Damor* | Gujarat HC | 28 years (injured, amputation) | Skilled workman (minimum wages) | **40%** | *Pranay Sethi* extended to permanent disablement cases (per *Pappu Deo Yadav*) |
| 4 | **doc_006** | *National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Smt. Meena* | Allahabad HC (Lucknow) | Between 40–50 years (government servant) | Permanent job (government) | **30%** | *Pranay Sethi* para 61(iii) — permanent job, age 40–50 |
| 5 | **doc_004** | *Oriental Insurance Co. v. Soma Devi* | Himachal Pradesh HC | 21 years | Self-employed/fixed salary | **40%** | *Pranay Sethi* para 59.4 — self-employed, below 40 |
| 6 | **doc_001** | *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Neelam Devi* | Punjab & Haryana HC | 22 years (Sultan) / 32 years (Munish) | Self-employed/fixed salary | **40%** (both) | *Pranay Sethi* — self-employed/fixed salary, below 40 |

---

### B. Judgments that cite *Pranay Sethi* but DO NOT apply future prospects

| Doc ID | Case Name | Reason for Non-Application |
|--------|-----------|---------------------------|
| **doc_011** | *Asfaq Ahmad v. Satender* | Deceased's income not proved; notional income used. Tribunal held: *"petitioners are not entitled for compensation towards future prospects"* following *Laxmidhar Nayak v. Juggal Kishore Behera*. |
| **doc_012** | *Smt. Rekha Kumari v. Himachal Road* | Injured claimant did not prove regular job/self-employment. Tribunal held: *"he is not entitled for addition towards future prospects"* — only notional income used. |

---

### C. The *Pranay Sethi* Framework (as applied in these judgments)

The percentages, as extracted verbatim in **doc_006** (quoting *Pranay Sethi* para 61):

**For permanent employment:**
| Age | Addition |
|-----|----------|
| Below 40 years | **50%** of actual salary (less tax) |
| 40 to 50 years | **30%** |
| 50 to 60 years | **15%** |

**For self-employed or fixed salary:**
| Age | Addition |
|-----|----------|
| Below 40 years | **40%** of established income (less tax) |
| 40 to 50 years | **25%** |
| 50 to 60 years | **10%** |

No addition is made where the deceased is above 60 years, or where the income is merely notional (unproven).

---

### Summary

- **50%** applied in: **doc_041** (permanent job, below 40)
- **40%** applied in: **doc_019**, **doc_020**, **doc_004**, **doc_001** (self-employed/fixed salary, below 40)
- **30%** applied in: **doc_006** (government servant, age 40–50)
- **Not applied** (notional income only): **doc_011**, **doc_012**

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1
supporting.principle: For a deceased below 40 years in stable employment with regular income, 50% of actual income must be added towards future prospects under Pranay Sethi.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased was below 40 and in stable employment (regular salary). The tribunal applied 50% addition.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes the highest future-prospects addition (50%) for permanent employees below 40, directly applying Pranay Sethi para 61(iii).
supporting.quote: 50% of actual salary should be added to the actual salary income of the deceased towards future prospects, where the deceased had a permanent job and was below 40 years.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: For self-employed or fixed-salary deceased below 40 years, 40% addition applies; for age 40-50, 25%; for 50-60, 10%.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 23 (first case) and 27 (second case), both on fixed salary. The court applied 40% addition.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Allahabad High Court judgment is the most detailed exposition of Pranay Sethi's future prospects framework in the corpus, applying the 40/25/10 sliding scale for non-permanent workers.
supporting.quote: Compensation on account of future prospects in such case may be computed at the rate of 40% of the established income in case of the age of the deceased being below 40 years; at the rate of 25%... between 40 to 50 years and at the rate of 10% in case of age... between 50 to 60 years.

supporting.title: Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria vs Dilipkumar Ranchhodbhai Damor
supporting.principle: Future prospects under Pranay Sethi apply not only to death cases but also to permanent disablement cases involving serious injuries.
supporting.fact_alignment: Claimant aged 28 with amputation of right leg below knee. The court applied 40% future prospects on minimum-wage income.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends Pranay Sethi's future prospects to injury/disablement cases, citing Pappu Deo Yadav. Important for claimants with permanent disabilities.
supporting.quote: This Court is inclined to consider 40% towards the future rise of income.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: For a government servant aged 40-50 years, 30% addition towards future prospects applies under Pranay Sethi.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased was a government servant aged between 40-50. The court applied 30% addition as per Pranay Sethi para 61(iii).
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the 30% bracket for permanent employees aged 40-50, and reproduces the full Pranay Sethi para 61 verbatim.
supporting.quote: If the deceased was a government servant and his age was between 40 to 50 years then 30% of his income should be added towards future prospects.

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: For a self-employed deceased below 40, 40% addition towards future prospects applies.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 21, self-employed. The court applied 40% addition under Pranay Sethi para 59.4.
supporting.why_it_matters: Himachal Pradesh HC applies the 40% bracket for self-employed below 40 and reproduces the full Pranay Sethi framework.
supporting.quote: In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 40% of the established income should be the warrant where the deceased was below the age of 40 years.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For self-employed/fixed-salary deceased below 40, 40% future prospects applies.
supporting.fact_alignment: Two deceased: Sultan aged 22 (40% applied) and Munish aged 32 (40% applied). Both treated as self-employed/fixed salary.
supporting.why_it_matters: Punjab & Haryana HC confirms 40% addition for self-employed/fixed-salary deceased below 40, and applies it even when the insurance company appealed (no cross-objections by claimants).
supporting.quote: By relying upon the authority cited in National Insurance Company Limited versus Pranay Sethi and Ors., the future prospects have to be considered... to the extent of 40%.

adverse.title: Asfaq Ahmad Father vs Satender & Ors
adverse.principle: Where the deceased's income is not proved and only notional income is used, future prospects are NOT awarded.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer will cite this to argue that if the claimant fails to prove the deceased's actual/established income (e.g., using only minimum wages without proof of employment), no future prospects addition is permissible.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the complete absence of proof of income or employment. Where the claimant produces salary slips, ITRs, or other documentary evidence of the deceased's income, future prospects must be added. The bar applies only to notional/unproven income cases.
adverse.quote: There is nothing on record to show that deceased was self employed or working in fixed salary; nothing is proved in respect of income of the deceased. In view of judgment... petitioners are not entitled for compensation towards future prospects.

adverse.title: Smt. Rekha Kumari W/O Late Sh. Sachin vs Himachal Road
adverse.principle: An injured claimant who does not prove regular employment or self-employment is not entitled to future prospects addition.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer will cite this to resist future prospects in injury cases where the claimant's employment status is unproven or the income is assessed on minimum wages without proof of the nature of work.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In doc_012, the injured claimant produced no documents to show regular job or self-employment. Where the claimant does prove employment (e.g., through appointment letters, salary slips, or business records), future prospects must be added. Doc_020 (Yogeshkumar) is the counter-authority: even on minimum wages, if the nature of work is established, 40% applies.
adverse.quote: The petitioner/injured did not produce any document to show that he was engaged in regular job / self employed... he is not entitled for addition towards future prospects.

adverse.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
adverse.principle: Where the tribunal uses notional income (minimum wages without proof of actual earnings), future prospects may not be separately added.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer may argue that where the tribunal notionally fixes income (as here, Rs. 100/day), no future prospects addition is warranted because the income itself is an estimate.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In doc_018, the court did not disturb the award because the claimants did not appeal. The judgment does not hold that future prospects cannot be added to notional income — it simply confirms the tribunal's award as passed. Pranay Sethi itself requires 'established income' (income minus tax), which can include minimum-wage income where the nature of work is proved (see doc_020).
adverse.quote: The learned MACT did not find the income of the deceased... proved by evidences. Therefore, on the then prevailing rate, Rs. 100/- was taken as minimum income.

priority_arguments: Lead with the Pranay Sethi framework (doc_006 reproduces para 61 verbatim) to establish the applicable percentages by age and employment type.
For permanent employees below 40: cite doc_041 for 50% addition.
For self-employed/fixed-salary below 40: cite doc_019, doc_004, and doc_001 for 40% addition.
For government servants aged 40-50: cite doc_006 for 30% addition.
For permanent disablement/injury cases: cite doc_020 (Yogeshkumar) to extend Pranay Sethi's future prospects to living claimants with serious injuries.

Pre-empt the 'no future prospects on notional income' argument by distinguishing doc_011 and doc_012: those cases had zero proof of employment/income. Where any documentary evidence exists (salary slips, ITRs, minimum-wage notifications with proof of work type), future prospects must be added.
strategy.compensation_range: Depends on the income, age, and employment type. The percentages are: 50% (permanent, below 40); 30% (permanent, 40-50); 15% (permanent, 50-60); 40% (self-employed/fixed, below 40); 25% (self-employed/fixed, 40-50); 10% (self-employed/fixed, 50-60). No addition above 60 or for notional/unproven income.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Use compute_quantum tool for exact figures. The framework is: (established monthly income + future prospects %) × 12 × multiplier (per Sarla Verma table) minus personal expense deduction (per Sarla Verma paras 30-32), plus conventional heads (loss of estate Rs. 15,000, loss of consortium Rs. 40,000, funeral expenses Rs. 15,000, enhanced 10% every 3 years per Pranay Sethi).
risks: Risk 1: If the claimant cannot prove the deceased's actual income or employment (only notional income), future prospects may be denied — doc_011 and doc_012 are adverse on this point.

Risk 2: Insurers may argue that minimum-wage income without proof of the nature of work does not constitute 'established income' — counter with doc_020 where the court applied 40% on minimum wages for a skilled workman.
Risk 3: For injury claims, some tribunals may resist extending Pranay Sethi beyond death cases — counter with doc_020 and the Supreme Court's Pappu Deo Yadav reasoning cited therein.

Risk 4: The 10% triennial enhancement on conventional heads (per Pranay Sethi para 61(viii)) may be disputed for accidents predating the judgment — doc_004 shows the court did not apply the enhancement for a 2010 accident.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act, with appeal to the High Court under Section 173 MV Act if the tribunal fails to apply future prospects. Where the tribunal has ignored future prospects despite proof of income, invoke Order 41 Rule 33 CPC in appeal (as in doc_004 and doc_019) to seek enhancement even without cross-objections.

caveats: doc_010 (Raju Gupta) cites Pranay Sethi but deals with injury compensation and disability assessment, not future prospects percentages — the tribunal did not apply future prospects because the claimant's employment was not proved.
doc_022 (Sangeeta Devi) uses notional income for a child deceased; future prospects were not applied — this is consistent with Pranay Sethi which requires 'established income'.

doc_033 (Satto & Ors), doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket), doc_028 (United India v. Sukumarbai), and doc_031 (National Insurance v. Laxmi Narain Dhut) cite Pranay Sethi only for insurer liability/recovery issues, not for future prospects percentages.

args.question: Which judgments apply future prospects under Pranay Sethi, and at what percentage?

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1
supporting.principle: For a deceased below 40 years in stable employment with regular income, 50% of actual income must be added towards future prospects under Pranay Sethi.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased was below 40 and in stable employment (regular salary). The tribunal applied 50% addition.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes the highest future-prospects addition (50%) for permanent employees below 40, directly applying Pranay Sethi para 61(iii).
supporting.quote: 50% of actual salary should be added to the actual salary income of the deceased towards future prospects, where the deceased had a permanent job and was below 40 years.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: For self-employed or fixed-salary deceased below 40 years, 40% addition applies; for age 40-50, 25%; for 50-60, 10%.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 23 (first case) and 27 (second case), both on fixed salary. The court applied 40% addition.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Allahabad High Court judgment is the most detailed exposition of Pranay Sethi's future prospects framework in the corpus, applying the 40/25/10 sliding scale for non-permanent workers.
supporting.quote: Compensation on account of future prospects in such case may be computed at the rate of 40% of the established income in case of the age of the deceased being below 40 years; at the rate of 25%... between 40 to 50 years and at the rate of 10% in case of age... between 50 to 60 years.

supporting.title: Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria vs Dilipkumar Ranchhodbhai Damor
supporting.principle: Future prospects under Pranay Sethi apply not only to death cases but also to permanent disablement cases involving serious injuries.
supporting.fact_alignment: Claimant aged 28 with amputation of right leg below knee. The court applied 40% future prospects on minimum-wage income.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends Pranay Sethi's future prospects to injury/disablement cases, citing Pappu Deo Yadav. Important for claimants with permanent disabilities.
supporting.quote: This Court is inclined to consider 40% towards the future rise of income.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: For a government servant aged 40-50 years, 30% addition towards future prospects applies under Pranay Sethi.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased was a government servant aged between 40-50. The court applied 30% addition as per Pranay Sethi para 61(iii).
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the 30% bracket for permanent employees aged 40-50, and reproduces the full Pranay Sethi para 61 verbatim.
supporting.quote: If the deceased was a government servant and his age was between 40 to 50 years then 30% of his income should be added towards future prospects.

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: For a self-employed deceased below 40, 40% addition towards future prospects applies.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 21, self-employed. The court applied 40% addition under Pranay Sethi para 59.4.
supporting.why_it_matters: Himachal Pradesh HC applies the 40% bracket for self-employed below 40 and reproduces the full Pranay Sethi framework.
supporting.quote: In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 40% of the established income should be the warrant where the deceased was below the age of 40 years.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For self-employed/fixed-salary deceased below 40, 40% future prospects applies.
supporting.fact_alignment: Two deceased: Sultan aged 22 (40% applied) and Munish aged 32 (40% applied). Both treated as self-employed/fixed salary.
supporting.why_it_matters: Punjab & Haryana HC confirms 40% addition for self-employed/fixed-salary deceased below 40, and applies it even when the insurance company appealed (no cross-objections by claimants).
supporting.quote: By relying upon the authority cited in National Insurance Company Limited versus Pranay Sethi and Ors., the future prospects have to be considered... to the extent of 40%.

adverse.title: Asfaq Ahmad Father vs Satender & Ors
adverse.principle: Where the deceased's income is not proved and only notional income is used, future prospects are NOT awarded.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer will cite this to argue that if the claimant fails to prove the deceased's actual/established income (e.g., using only minimum wages without proof of employment), no future prospects addition is permissible.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the complete absence of proof of income or employment. Where the claimant produces salary slips, ITRs, or other documentary evidence of the deceased's income, future prospects must be added. The bar applies only to notional/unproven income cases.
adverse.quote: There is nothing on record to show that deceased was self employed or working in fixed salary; nothing is proved in respect of income of the deceased. In view of judgment... petitioners are not entitled for compensation towards future prospects.

adverse.title: Smt. Rekha Kumari W/O Late Sh. Sachin vs Himachal Road
adverse.principle: An injured claimant who does not prove regular employment or self-employment is not entitled to future prospects addition.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer will cite this to resist future prospects in injury cases where the claimant's employment status is unproven or the income is assessed on minimum wages without proof of the nature of work.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In doc_012, the injured claimant produced no documents to show regular job or self-employment. Where the claimant does prove employment (e.g., through appointment letters, salary slips, or business records), future prospects must be added. Doc_020 (Yogeshkumar) is the counter-authority: even on minimum wages, if the nature of work is established, 40% applies.
adverse.quote: The petitioner/injured did not produce any document to show that he was engaged in regular job / self employed... he is not entitled for addition towards future prospects.

adverse.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
adverse.principle: Where the tribunal uses notional income (minimum wages without proof of actual earnings), future prospects may not be separately added.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer may argue that where the tribunal notionally fixes income (as here, Rs. 100/day), no future prospects addition is warranted because the income itself is an estimate.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In doc_018, the court did not disturb the award because the claimants did not appeal. The judgment does not hold that future prospects cannot be added to notional income — it simply confirms the tribunal's award as passed. Pranay Sethi itself requires 'established income' (income minus tax), which can include minimum-wage income where the nature of work is proved (see doc_020).
adverse.quote: The learned MACT did not find the income of the deceased... proved by evidences. Therefore, on the then prevailing rate, Rs. 100/- was taken as minimum income.

priority_arguments: Lead with the Pranay Sethi framework (doc_006 reproduces para 61 verbatim) to establish the applicable percentages by age and employment type.
For permanent employees below 40: cite doc_041 for 50% addition.
For self-employed/fixed-salary below 40: cite doc_019, doc_004, and doc_001 for 40% addition.
For government servants aged 40-50: cite doc_006 for 30% addition.
For permanent disablement/injury cases: cite doc_020 (Yogeshkumar) to extend Pranay Sethi's future prospects to living claimants with serious injuries.

Pre-empt the 'no future prospects on notional income' argument by distinguishing doc_011 and doc_012: those cases had zero proof of employment/income. Where any documentary evidence exists (salary slips, ITRs, minimum-wage notifications with proof of work type), future prospects must be added.
strategy.compensation_range: Depends on the income, age, and employment type. The percentages are: 50% (permanent, below 40); 30% (permanent, 40-50); 15% (permanent, 50-60); 40% (self-employed/fixed, below 40); 25% (self-employed/fixed, 40-50); 10% (self-employed/fixed, 50-60). No addition above 60 or for notional/unproven income.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Use compute_quantum tool for exact figures. The framework is: (established monthly income + future prospects %) × 12 × multiplier (per Sarla Verma table) minus personal expense deduction (per Sarla Verma paras 30-32), plus conventional heads (loss of estate Rs. 15,000, loss of consortium Rs. 40,000, funeral expenses Rs. 15,000, enhanced 10% every 3 years per Pranay Sethi).
risks: Risk 1: If the claimant cannot prove the deceased's actual income or employment (only notional income), future prospects may be denied — doc_011 and doc_012 are adverse on this point.

Risk 2: Insurers may argue that minimum-wage income without proof of the nature of work does not constitute 'established income' — counter with doc_020 where the court applied 40% on minimum wages for a skilled workman.
Risk 3: For injury claims, some tribunals may resist extending Pranay Sethi beyond death cases — counter with doc_020 and the Supreme Court's Pappu Deo Yadav reasoning cited therein.

Risk 4: The 10% triennial enhancement on conventional heads (per Pranay Sethi para 61(viii)) may be disputed for accidents predating the judgment — doc_004 shows the court did not apply the enhancement for a 2010 accident.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act, with appeal to the High Court under Section 173 MV Act if the tribunal fails to apply future prospects. Where the tribunal has ignored future prospects despite proof of income, invoke Order 41 Rule 33 CPC in appeal (as in doc_004 and doc_019) to seek enhancement even without cross-objections.

caveats: doc_017 (Sanjay v. State of Haryana) is a criminal revision petition about rash driving conviction and sentencing under IPC. It has nothing to do with compensation quantum or future prospects under Pranay Sethi. Not relevant.

doc_023 (Suman Lata v. Madan Mohan Sonkar) is a pre-Pranay Sethi judgment (2005) that discusses future prospects under the pre-Sarla Verma framework (Susamma Thomas / Sarla Dixit line). It does not apply Pranay Sethi percentages and is not adverse on the question asked.
doc_051 (Yashpal Chaudhrani v. State) is a criminal quashing petition about economic frauds and credit card offences. Entirely unrelated to motor accident compensation or future prospects.
doc_054 (Chinnasamy v. K.Viswanathan) is a civil second appeal about specific performance of a sale agreement. No connection to motor accidents or future prospects.
doc_055 (Iravva K Purantar v. S Venkatesh) is a civil first appeal about specific performance and impleadment. No connection to motor accident compensation.

doc_010 (Raju Gupta v. Himachal Road) cites Pranay Sethi but deals with injury compensation and disability assessment — the tribunal did not apply future prospects because the claimant's employment was not proved. Not adverse; fact-specific.

payload.holding: The tribunal held that the insurer proved a fundamental breach of policy conditions due to the driver lacking a valid driving licence, but directed the insurer to pay the compensation to the petitioner in the first instance under the 'pay and recover' principle, with liberty to recover the same from the vehicle owner.
payload.ratio: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.

payload.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
payload.court: In The High Court Of Judicature At Bombay Bench At Aurangabad
payload.holding: The Tribunal erred in passing an order of 'pay and recover' against the insurance company when passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward are not third parties and their risk is not covered under the Act policy, and therefore the insurer is completely exonerated.
payload.ratio: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and the Tribunal or Court cannot invoke 'pay and recover' to compel the insurer to satisfy the award and recover from the owner.

Thus, the Hon'ble Supreme Court had taken a note of the fact that the Tribunal had directed the
insurance company to pay compensation and then to recover it from the owner, but when the High
Court had 12 FA_2021_2018_Jd interfered it, the said fact of exonerating the insurance company
by the High Court was not approved. However, it is to be noted that Shamanna's case, was a case,
where there was no valid and effective driving licence and therefore, it was held that, it was a breach
of terms of policy. Deceased therein was considered as 'third party' and then on the ground of
breach of term in respect of driving licence, the order of pay and recovered held to be justified.
14 Further, note can be taken of the decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court in New India Assurance
Company Ltd. Vs. Asha Rani [AIR 2003 SC 607]. It has been laid down that the term "any person"
used in Section 147 of the Motor Vehicle Act mean "third Party" but not passenger.

args.question: Which judgments apply future prospects under Pranay Sethi, and at what percentage?

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1
supporting.principle: For a deceased below 40 years in stable employment with regular income, 50% of actual income must be added towards future prospects under Pranay Sethi.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased was below 40 and in stable employment (regular salary). The tribunal applied 50% addition.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes the highest future-prospects addition (50%) for permanent employees below 40, directly applying Pranay Sethi para 61(iii).
supporting.quote: 50% of actual salary should be added to the actual salary income of the deceased towards future prospects, where the deceased had a permanent job and was below 40 years.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: For self-employed or fixed-salary deceased below 40 years, 40% addition applies; for age 40-50, 25%; for 50-60, 10%.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 23 (first case) and 27 (second case), both on fixed salary. The court applied 40% addition.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Allahabad High Court judgment is the most detailed exposition of Pranay Sethi's future prospects framework in the corpus, applying the 40/25/10 sliding scale for non-permanent workers.
supporting.quote: Compensation on account of future prospects in such case may be computed at the rate of 40% of the established income in case of the age of the deceased being below 40 years; at the rate of 25%... between 40 to 50 years and at the rate of 10% in case of age... between 50 to 60 years.

supporting.title: Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria vs Dilipkumar Ranchhodbhai Damor
supporting.principle: Future prospects under Pranay Sethi apply not only to death cases but also to permanent disablement cases involving serious injuries.
supporting.fact_alignment: Claimant aged 28 with amputation of right leg below knee. The court applied 40% future prospects on minimum-wage income.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends Pranay Sethi's future prospects to injury/disablement cases, citing Pappu Deo Yadav. Important for claimants with permanent disabilities.
supporting.quote: This Court is inclined to consider 40% towards the future rise of income.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: For a government servant aged 40-50 years, 30% addition towards future prospects applies under Pranay Sethi.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased was a government servant aged between 40-50. The court applied 30% addition as per Pranay Sethi para 61(iii).
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the 30% bracket for permanent employees aged 40-50, and reproduces the full Pranay Sethi para 61 verbatim.
supporting.quote: If the deceased was a government servant and his age was between 40 to 50 years then 30% of his income should be added towards future prospects.

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: For a self-employed deceased below 40, 40% addition towards future prospects applies.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 21, self-employed. The court applied 40% addition under Pranay Sethi para 59.4.
supporting.why_it_matters: Himachal Pradesh HC applies the 40% bracket for self-employed below 40 and reproduces the full Pranay Sethi framework.
supporting.quote: In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 40% of the established income should be the warrant where the deceased was below the age of 40 years.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For self-employed/fixed-salary deceased below 40, 40% future prospects applies.
supporting.fact_alignment: Two deceased: Sultan aged 22 (40% applied) and Munish aged 32 (40% applied). Both treated as self-employed/fixed salary.
supporting.why_it_matters: Punjab & Haryana HC confirms 40% addition for self-employed/fixed-salary deceased below 40, and applies it even when the insurance company appealed (no cross-objections by claimants).
supporting.quote: By relying upon the authority cited in National Insurance Company Limited versus Pranay Sethi and Ors., the future prospects have to be considered... to the extent of 40%.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Future prospects under Pranay Sethi apply to permanent disablement cases; 40% addition for a claimant aged 25.
supporting.fact_alignment: Claimant aged 25 with 100% disability. The tribunal applied 40% future prospects on notional income of Rs. 15,000/month, citing Pappu Deo Yadav and Pranay Sethi.
supporting.why_it_matters: A MACT judgment that applies 40% future prospects in a serious injury case, reinforcing doc_020. Also shows that even on notional income (where no documentary proof exists), future prospects can be added if the disability is serious.
supporting.quote: By applying the principle laid down in Pappu Deo Yadav's case... this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that while awarding compensation under the head of future loss of income it is proper to add future prospects as scheduled in Pranay Sethi's case.

adverse.title: Asfaq Ahmad Father vs Satender & Ors
adverse.principle: Where the deceased's income is not proved and only notional income is used, future prospects are NOT awarded.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer will cite this to argue that if the claimant fails to prove the deceased's actual/established income (e.g., using only minimum wages without proof of employment), no future prospects addition is permissible.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the complete absence of proof of income or employment. Where the claimant produces salary slips, ITRs, or other documentary evidence of the deceased's income, future prospects must be added. The bar applies only to notional/unproven income cases.
adverse.quote: There is nothing on record to show that deceased was self employed or working in fixed salary; nothing is proved in respect of income of the deceased. In view of judgment... petitioners are not entitled for compensation towards future prospects.

adverse.title: Smt. Rekha Kumari W/O Late Sh. Sachin vs Himachal Road
adverse.principle: An injured claimant who does not prove regular employment or self-employment is not entitled to future prospects addition.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer will cite this to resist future prospects in injury cases where the claimant's employment status is unproven or the income is assessed on minimum wages without proof of the nature of work.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In doc_012, the injured claimant produced no documents to show regular job or self-employment. Where the claimant does prove employment (e.g., through appointment letters, salary slips, or business records), future prospects must be added. Doc_020 (Yogeshkumar) and doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) are the counter-authorities: even on minimum wages/notional income, if the nature of work or disability is established, 40% applies.
adverse.quote: The petitioner/injured did not produce any document to show that he was engaged in regular job / self employed... he is not entitled for addition towards future prospects.

adverse.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
adverse.principle: Under the pre-Pranay Sethi framework (Reshma Kumari), a self-employed deceased or one in temporary employment is NOT entitled to any addition towards future prospects.
adverse.risk_to_client: An insurer will cite this to argue that for self-employed or temporary workers, future prospects should be zero — relying on the Reshma Kumari line which Pranay Sethi later overruled.
